reference_title: Design, Analysis, and Testing of Laterally Loaded Deep Foundations that Support Transportation Facilities

sections.title: Construction Management and Inspection
sections.summary: Lateral performance depends on reaching the minimum embedment, not disturbing the resisting ground, and building elements with the required strength and integrity. Knowledgeable inspection and response to unanticipated conditions are essential; roles in Hannigan et al. (2016) and Brown et al. (2010).
sections.body: Successful construction of foundation elements for lateral load resistance depends on (a) achieving the minimum embedment established by the designer, (b) avoiding disturbance of the geo-materials around the element relied on for lateral resistance, and (c) constructing the elements with the required structural strength and integrity. Knowledgeable supervision and inspection is essential, as is recognizing and responding to unanticipated site conditions that could adversely affect lateral performance. Inspection roles and responsibilities are discussed in Hannigan et al. (2016) for driven piles and Brown et al. (2010) for drilled shafts; considerations specific to laterally loaded foundations follow in the chapter. (p. 197)
key_points: Reach the minimum embedment set by the designer (p. 197).
Avoid disturbing the ground relied on for lateral resistance (p. 197).
Build elements with the required structural strength and integrity (p. 197).
Inspection roles: Hannigan et al. (2016), Brown et al. (2010) (p. 197).
sections.applicability: Construction management and inspection oversight for laterally loaded deep foundations

sections.title: Constructability Review
sections.summary: Before construction, review constructibility and mitigate risks: element size and type, site constraints, achievable depths (driveability analysis for piles, tools for shafts), installation and third-party risks, sequence, a representative load test area, remedies, and alternatives compared by cost and risk. Reviewers need construction experience.
sections.body: Before construction the design should be reviewed to verify it is constructible with available means and methods, identifying and mitigating risks where possible. Considerations may include: (1) appropriate foundation size and type: a. pile sizes and lengths suited to the pile type (dimension, steel section, thickness), splicing and its schedule impact; b. drilled shaft diameters reasonable for the project size and contractor pool, large shafts possibly inappropriate on small local projects; (2) installability within site constraints (working area, slopes, headroom, access, equipment support); (3) whether the proposed depths can be reached in the bearing strata, and risks of obstructions or rock: a. a driveability analysis generally for driven piles; b. tool changes or specialty tools for hard layers or obstructions for drilled shafts; (4) installation risks such as vibration settlement, excavation instability (drilled shafts, CFAs), contaminated spoils; (5) risks to third parties, nearby structures, public complaints or community impacts; (6) a technically and economically feasible construction sequence; (7) for required load tests, an area representative of the site as a whole (p. 198); (8) ways to resolve foreseeable problems should they occur; (9) for more than one viable alternative, cost estimates and constructability compared: the lowest cost alternative is not necessarily best if riskier, since a problem in construction may push its cost well above the lower risk alternative. Considerations vary with project size, location, local conditions and practice; the list is examples, not comprehensive, and the review should be performed by staff with appropriate construction experience. (pp. 197 to 198)
key_points: Verify the design is constructible; identify and mitigate risks (p. 197).
Check size and type, site constraints and achievable depths; driveability analysis for piles (p. 197).
Consider installation, third-party risks and sequence (p. 197).
Lowest cost alternative is not necessarily best if riskier (p. 198).
Review by staff with construction experience (p. 198).
sections.applicability: Pre-construction design review for constructability of laterally loaded deep foundations

sections.title: Design Considerations and Changes in Construction
sections.summary: Changes arise from contractor proposals (communicate lateral criteria and resistance factors), means and methods (e.g., pre-excavation reduces lateral resistance), construction-phase investigations (deferred exploration adds risk; design-build finalizes them), observed conditions (weaker ground, rock higher or lower), and construction load tests.
sections.body: Considerations and design changes during construction may include: (1) contractor value engineering or alternative design proposals on pre-construction data, a new design or a change in one aspect (pile type, shaft size); lateral design requirements (specifications, Strength and Service Limit State deflections) and required or suggested resistance factors should be clearly communicated; (2) review and approval of means and methods, which may affect lateral as well as axial capacity, e.g. pre-excavation to remove obstructions may reduce lateral resistance within its depth; (3) changes due to construction data from explorations and operations (foundation installation, excavation, groundwater control): a. construction-phase investigation: i. in design-bid-build, a contractor requirement, e.g. borings at inaccessible locations or at every drilled shaft to verify socket rock quality; deferring investigation adds significant risk, since differing conditions may force redesign affecting schedule and cost, so contracts should include means to pay for it and adjust foundation payment (p. 199); ii. contractor borings for temporary works, value engineering or a possible differing site condition; iii. in design-build, investigations to develop, finalize or optimize the design, the final program typically deferred until the design-build contractor's consultant sets foundation locations; b. deep foundation design inherently includes some observational method: i. weaker ground than anticipated (thicker weak strata, lower resistance from investigations, tests or driving records) may require re-evaluation, adjustment and construction testing including lateral load tests; ii. rock higher than the tip of non-socketed foundations (driven piles, CFA piles, shafts in soil) shortens them below lateral requirements, needing a size change, rock sockets or pre-drilling; rock lower than expected for socketed foundations resembles thicker weak overburden; c. lateral load tests in construction (required, or chosen by the contractor to optimize, more common in design-build, or for value engineering or claims in design-bid-build) verify or update the design for better or worse performance than anticipated. (pp. 198 to 199)
key_points: Communicate lateral criteria and resistance factors for contractor proposals (p. 198).
Means and methods matter: pre-excavation reduces lateral resistance (p. 198).
Deferred exploration in design-bid-build adds significant risk (p. 198).
Weaker ground or different rock levels may require redesign (p. 199).
Construction lateral load tests verify or update the design (p. 199).
sections.applicability: Managing design changes and construction data for laterally loaded deep foundations

sections.title: Driven Pile, Drilled Shaft, and Backfill Considerations
sections.summary: Introduces construction considerations for driven piles (13.4.2), drilled shafts (13.4.3), position and alignment (13.4.1), and backfill and grading (13.4.4).
sections.body: Specific construction considerations for driven piles, drilled shafts, and backfill and grading are discussed in the subsequent sections. (p. 199)
key_points: Covers position and alignment, driven piles, drilled shafts, backfill and grading (p. 199).
sections.applicability: Construction details for driven piles, drilled shafts, and site preparation to preserve lateral load performance

sections.title: Pile/Shaft Position and Alignment
sections.summary: Group and wall p-y multipliers depend on spacing, so install elements at design locations: clear obstructions, field-locate utilities, plan plumbness equipment, have the engineer-of-record approve adjustments and report out-of-tolerance elements promptly.
sections.body: Laterally loaded vertical elements in a group or at linear intervals (noise wall, top-down wall) are designed for overlapping passive influence zones with p-y multipliers from their spacing, so they must be installed at their design locations. To limit out-of-position or out-of-plumb installation, clear foundation locations of obstructions (abandoned foundations, tree roots); field locate buried pipes and utilities not accurately identified or relocated in advance, to find conflicts that may need redesign; have all field adjustments approved by the engineer-of-record; consider in advance the equipment accessories (pile leads, pre-bore augers, casing templates, rock chisels, boulder breakers) needed to keep elements plumb, consistent with the specifications; and promptly report elements out of tolerance for location or plumbness to the engineer-of-record. (p. 200)
key_points: p-y multipliers depend on spacing: install at design locations (p. 200).
Clear obstructions; field locate utilities (p. 200).
Engineer-of-record approves field adjustments (p. 200).
Report out-of-tolerance elements promptly (p. 200).
sections.applicability: Construction details for driven piles, drilled shafts, and site preparation to preserve lateral load performance

sections.title: Driven Pile Installations
sections.summary: Installation means and methods can impair driven pile lateral resistance; general driven pile construction is in Hannigan et al. (2016), and the subsections give the considerations specific to laterally loaded piles.
sections.body: The utility of driven piles for lateral load resistance can be adversely affected by the means and methods of installation. Construction considerations for driven piles are discussed in detail in Hannigan et al. (2016); the following are specific to laterally loaded pile foundations. (p. 200)
key_points: Installation methods can reduce lateral resistance (p. 200).
General driven pile construction: Hannigan et al. (2016) (p. 200).
sections.applicability: Driven pile installation practices that preserve lateral load resistance

sections.title: Equipment Selection
sections.summary: Wave Equation Analysis drivability studies, by a knowledgeable specialist matching the contractor's system to the pile, ground and requirements, assess whether hammers can reach the minimum tip elevation for lateral resistance.
sections.body: Wave Equation Analysis (WEA) drivability studies are very useful for assessing whether impact hammers can install piles to at least the minimum tip elevation needed for the required lateral resistance. They should be conducted by a knowledgeable foundation specialist, matching the contractor's proposed driving system to the pile type, ground conditions and performance requirements. See Hannigan et al. (2016). (p. 200)
key_points: WEA drivability checks reaching the minimum tip elevation (p. 200).
By a knowledgeable specialist matching the proposed system (p. 200).
sections.applicability: Driven pile installation practices that preserve lateral load resistance

sections.title: Sequence of Driving
sections.summary: On slopes drive from top to bottom, since bottom-up driving displaces, tilts or bends installed piles; in groups drive interior piles first so densification does not stop later piles above plan depth.
sections.body: When driving piles on slopes such as a river bank, driving sequentially from the bottom to the top typically displaces, tilts and possibly bends previously installed piles, so installation should progress from top to bottom. Similarly, ground displacement favors driving the interior piles of a group first, reducing the risk that densification prevents later piles reaching plan depth, which may impair their function in bending. (p. 200)
key_points: On slopes, drive from top to bottom (p. 200).
In groups, drive interior piles first (p. 200).
sections.applicability: Driven pile installation practices that preserve lateral load resistance

sections.title: Driving Refusal
sections.summary: Refusal above the minimum tip elevation for lateral resistance (hard layers, boulders, high bedrock, densification) requires notifying the engineer-of-record; remedies include predrilling, spudding, resequencing, or changing the number or arrangement of piles.
sections.body: Piles may refuse above the plan minimum tip elevation for lateral resistance because of hard layers, boulders, unanticipated higher bedrock or densification from earlier piles. The engineer-of-record should then be notified to assess acceptance of the pile and whether measures are needed for later piles in the group: predrilling through a hard layer, spudding to break obstructions, changing the driving sequence, or modifying the number or arrangement of piles. (p. 201)
key_points: Refusal above minimum tip: notify the engineer-of-record (p. 201).
Remedies: predrilling, spudding, resequencing, more or rearranged piles (p. 201).
sections.applicability: Driven pile installation practices that preserve lateral load resistance

sections.title: Splicing
sections.summary: Steel pile splices should be full penetration groove welds by a certified welder; avoid partial-strength mechanical splices unless planned deep where moments are small; engineer-of-record approves field splices. Avoid splices in precast concrete piles.
sections.body: Piles may need driving deeper than the ordered length for axial resistance. Steel pile splices should be full penetration groove welds developing the full structural capacity, made by a qualified and experienced certified welder. Mechanical splices with less than full bending strength should be avoided unless the splice can be anticipated and located deep in the ground where bending moments are relatively small. Field splices should be approved by the engineer-of-record. Splices should generally be avoided for precast concrete piles, since typical splices may not develop full capacity and may be damaged by continued driving. (p. 201)
key_points: Steel splices: full penetration groove welds by a certified welder (p. 201).
Partial-strength mechanical splices only deep where moments are small (p. 201).
Avoid splices in precast concrete piles (p. 201).
sections.applicability: Driven pile installation practices that preserve lateral load resistance

sections.title: Jetting and Pre-boring
sections.summary: Jetting and pre-boring reduce axial and possibly lateral resistance by loosening soil; often precluded. Where allowed, limit depth and hole size (Hannigan et al. 2016: not more than 6 inches over the largest pile dimension); avoid unless allowed or approved by the engineer-of-record.
sections.body: Hard driving or vibration control may prompt jetting or pre-boring from the surface to a limited depth. Specifications sometimes preclude them because of unknown reduction in side resistance or, for jetting, settlement or undermining of adjacent piles or structures. Where allowed, pre-boring is usually limited in depth and in hole diameter relative to the pile, Hannigan et al. (2016) recommending a pre-bored hole not more than 6 inches larger than the largest pile dimension (printed "not more than 6 inches than"). Both reduce axial resistance (Hannigan et al. 2016) and may reduce lateral resistance by loosening soil around the pile, so they should be avoided unless allowed by the project documents or approved by the engineer-of-record. (p. 201)
key_points: Jetting and pre-boring may loosen soil and reduce lateral resistance (p. 201).
Pre-bored hole not more than 6 in. over the largest pile dimension (Hannigan et al. 2016) (p. 201).
Avoid unless allowed or approved by the engineer-of-record (p. 201).
sections.applicability: Driven pile installation practices that preserve lateral load resistance

sections.title: Drilled Shafts
sections.summary: General drilled shaft construction is in Brown et al. (2010); the subsections cover pre-drilling and casing, structural integrity and rock sockets as they bear on lateral performance.
sections.body: Numerous drilled shaft construction considerations are in Brown et al. (2010); those of particular importance to laterally loaded drilled shafts are discussed below. (p. 201)
key_points: General drilled shaft construction: Brown et al. (2010) (p. 201).
sections.applicability: Drilled shaft construction practices that preserve lateral load resistance

sections.title: Pre-Drilling and Surface Casing
sections.summary: Oversized pre-drilling or surface casing loosens soil outside the shaft. Below cut-off or scour depth keep the auger no larger than the shaft, loosen rather than remove, and fill voids with tamped granular backfill or grout; with oversized surface casing, clean it out so concrete fills the annulus, or backfill it around permanent casing.
sections.body: Pre-drilling, with or without removal, sometimes eases installing temporary or permanent casing; an auger larger than the casing may loosen material outside the shaft, no concern if pre-drilling stops at the shaft cut-off level or the design scour depth. Otherwise the pre-drilling auger should generally be no larger than the completed shaft, and pre-drilling limited to loosening rather than removing soil; if an oversized pre-drilled hole extends below cut-off, the contractor should fill voids around the casing with tamped granular backfill or grout before drilling on. An oversized surface casing can leave loosened material in the annulus between shaft and casing: the contractor can remove all soil within the surface casing before extending the shaft below it and let shaft concrete flow into the annulus as the temporary casing is pulled, keeping spoil out of the void; if permanent casing is installed within the surface casing, the annulus should be backfilled with tamped granular backfill or grout. (p. 202)
key_points: Oversized pre-drilling below cut-off or scour depth loosens soil (p. 202).
Auger no larger than the completed shaft; loosen rather than remove (p. 202).
Fill voids with tamped granular backfill or grout (p. 202).
Clean out oversized surface casing so concrete fills the annulus (p. 202).
sections.applicability: Drilled shaft construction practices that preserve lateral load resistance

sections.title: Structural Integrity
sections.summary: Concrete defects (necking, honeycombing, soil intrusion, segregation, bleed channels, low strength, laitance, cold joints) reduce stiffness and increase lateral displacement. Verify by CSL (ASTM D6760) or SE/IR (ASTM D5882), less often GGL or TIP (ASTM D7949); confirm anomalies by coring or inspection; remediate or add shafts.
sections.body: Structural integrity of the shaft concrete is a major concern: poor placement or inappropriate mixes can cause defects that reduce stiffness and increase lateral displacement, and greatly reduce axial integrity. Common defects include necking, honeycombing, soil intrusion, segregation of aggregates, bleed-water channels, low strength concrete, laitance and cold joints. NDT methods typically specified are Crosshole Sonic Logging (CSL, ASTM D6760) and Sonic Echo / Impulse Response (SE/IR, ASTM D5882); less common are Gamma-Gamma Logging (GGL, California Department of Transportation Test No. 233) and Thermal Integrity Profiling (TIP, ASTM D7949), each with advantages and disadvantages (Brown et al. 2010). They identify anomalies (potential defects) warranting concrete coring or, near the top, visual inspection of the exposed shaft; confirmed defects that significantly affect performance can be remediated (Brown et al. 2010) or additional shafts installed to replace or supplement the defective shaft. (p. 202)
key_points: Concrete defects reduce stiffness and increase lateral displacement (p. 202).
NDT: CSL (ASTM D6760), SE/IR (ASTM D5882), GGL, TIP (ASTM D7949) (p. 202).
Investigate anomalies by coring or inspection (p. 202).
Remediate or add shafts for significant defects (p. 202).
sections.applicability: Drilled shaft construction practices that preserve lateral load resistance

sections.title: Rock Sockets
sections.summary: Rock socket fixity gives high lateral resistance only if top of rock and rock quality match design, which can vary sharply. Investigate per Chapter 3; for highly loaded or non-redundant shafts require a rock core boring at each shaft before drilling, typically in the construction contract.
sections.body: Drilled shafts and other drilled-in types such as micropiles can develop high lateral resistance from fixity in a rock socket, but the designer must verify that the top of rock elevation and rock quality are consistent with design assumptions; in some geologic settings both vary dramatically over short distances, and appreciably different conditions can delay work while the engineer-of-record evaluates them. To reduce delays and costly changes, an appropriate design-phase investigation (Chapter 3) should define rock conditions, and projects with highly loaded or non-redundant drilled shafts should require a rock core boring at each shaft location ahead of drilling, giving the designer time to confirm or adjust socket depth and length and the contractor time to fabricate cages; these borings are typically in the construction contract and done before shaft installation. (p. 203)
key_points: Socket fixity depends on top of rock and rock quality matching design (p. 203).
Rock surface and quality can vary sharply over short distances (p. 203).
Design-phase investigation per Chapter 3 (p. 203).
Highly loaded or non-redundant shafts: a rock core boring at each shaft (p. 203).
sections.applicability: Drilled shaft construction practices that preserve lateral load resistance

sections.title: Backfill and Grading
sections.summary: Build new embankments before installing foundations (pre-bore driven piles through compacted fill); if foundations come first, use small lifts and hand compaction. Slope fill to drain, place backfill in contact, and preload soft ground first to avoid lateral soil displacement (downdrag may still develop).
sections.body: When foundations are installed through (printed "though") a new embankment, the embankment is often specified to be built first, easing fill placement and compaction and avoiding damage or displacement of the elements; driven piles through compacted fill commonly require pre-boring to ease driving and keep alignment. If foundations must be installed before the embankment, e.g. behind an MSE wall, fill is placed in smaller lifts compacted with hand operated equipment. Fill around the elements should slope to drain away, and backfill should be placed in contact with the foundation to avoid loose zones and prevent ponding or infiltration that can soften or erode soil and degrade lateral support. Where soft compressible soils underlie the embankment, preloading to eliminate or substantially reduce settlement before installation is usually recommended; it may not reduce design downdrag (small relative settlement can develop full downdrag) but protects the elements from lateral soil displacements, and related deformation and bending stresses, near the preload perimeter. (p. 203)
key_points: Build embankments before foundations; pre-bore driven piles through compacted fill (p. 203).
Foundations first: small lifts, hand compaction (p. 203).
Slope fill to drain; backfill in contact with the foundation (p. 203).
Preload soft ground first to avoid lateral soil displacement; downdrag may still develop (p. 203).
sections.applicability: Construction details for driven piles, drilled shafts, and site preparation to preserve lateral load performance
